title: How A First-Day-Of-School Lesson Can Improve Classroom Management For The Rest Of The Year ve-classroom-management-for-the-rest-of-the-year/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a detailed, single-lesson strategy for setting an exceptionally high standard of excellence on the very first day of school, using an everyday task like the morning entry routine as the vehicle. The core idea is to teach a routine with obsessive, minute detail, redefining what students consider 'normal' performance in a way that transfers to behavior, motivation, and politeness throughout the year. He lays out a four-phase teaching sequence: the teacher models the routine precisely, using a borrowed backpack to demonstrate purpose and concentration; a single student then models it while classmates visualize doing the same; several more students model individually, with corrections and restarts for any missed steps; and finally the whole class performs the routine simultaneously outdoors, with the teacher only observing and resisting the urge to talk them through it. He stresses that students are unusually receptive to a reset on the first day, and that once this new standard is proven achievable, the teacher should confidently and enthusiastically affirm that it has been done perfectly, since believing excellence is attainable is itself part of the lesson.
points: Teaching one everyday routine with obsessive, highly detailed precision on day one resets students' baseline definition of excellence.
The first day of school is when students are most receptive to a new standard, since they are primed to start fresh.
The four-phase teaching sequence — teacher models, one student models, several students model, then the whole class performs together — builds mastery gradually.
Teachers should resist talking students through the routine once it's underway, to build independence and confidence.
Once students perform a routine correctly, teachers should confidently affirm it as perfect rather than implying there's always more to improve.
quotes: You see, one of the best things you can do on the first day of school is set the bar of what is normal far above what your students are used to.
Furthermore, on the first day of school your students will be more open to change than at any other time during the year.

The way the strategy works is that you’re going to teach your students a common, everyday routine—like how to enter the classroom in the morning—in a way that is highly, minutely, even obsessively, detailed.
Borrow a student’s backpack and, while pretending to be an actual member of your class, perform the morning routine precisely how you want your students to do it.
Resist the urge to talk them through the routine—which will weaken rather than strengthen performance and create dependency on you.
When they finish, if they get it right, be sure and tell them that it’s perfect, that it can’t be done any better. Many teachers are afraid to do this.
